reading.title: Keeping Trains on Winter Tracks
reading.purpose: Learn how engineers use physics and smart tools to keep rail lines moving in freezing weather.
paras: On a clear morning, a heavy train rolls smoothly along steel rails. In January, ice and freezing wind turn that simple ride into a difficult engineering test. Cold weather changes how metal behaves. Steel rails contract when temperatures drop, shrinking slightly and pulling tight at every joint. If crews do not leave tiny gaps during installation, the tension can snap a bolt or bend a switch.

Grip is an even bigger concern. A locomotive needs strong traction, the firm hold between wheel and rail that keeps steel from spinning in place. Wet leaves, frost, and packed snow reduce that grip. To solve this problem, many trains carry sandboxes above the wheels. When sensors detect slipping, a pipe drops fine grit onto the rail. Drivers stay alert and avoid anything that might distract them from the gauges, because a single missed warning can add hundreds of feet to a stop.

Winter delays can quickly become protracted, stretching far longer than a quick storm. Crews work along the line to extract packed ice from switch points, pulling hard chunks out before a rail locks shut. Some rail yards install small heaters that keep switches clear. Others use metal brushes that extend when snow falls and retract back under the train once the track is clean. Even a small failure can detract from riders' trust in public transit.

To plan repairs, dispatchers do not rely on abstract guesses or vague ideas about the weather. They measure real temperatures, track speeds, and subtract lost minutes from each route schedule to see where backups form. Ice storms can feel intractable, stubborn and hard to manage, yet steady maintenance keeps most trains moving. By studying how cold pulls on metal and wheels, rail teams turn winter's grip into a problem they can solve.

qs.q: In paragraph 1, the word "contract" most nearly means
choices: to sign a formal agreement with a builder
to shrink slightly and pull tighter together
to slide rapidly down a frozen metal slope
to melt into a soft liquid under high heat
qs.why: Paragraph 1 defines it directly: steel rails contract by "shrinking slightly and pulling tight at every joint."

qs.q: Which sentence explains how a train restores grip when its wheels begin to slip?
choices: A locomotive needs strong traction, the firm hold between wheel and rail that keeps steel from spinning in place.
Wet leaves, frost, and packed snow reduce that grip.
When sensors detect slipping, a pipe drops fine grit onto the rail.
Drivers stay alert and avoid anything that might distract them from the gauges, because a single missed warning can add hundreds of feet to a stop.
qs.why: This sentence describes the exact action taken when slipping occurs: a pipe drops fine grit onto the rail.

ev.text: When sensors detect slipping, a pipe drops fine grit onto the rail.

qs.q: What happens to the metal brushes on some trains after the snow is cleared?
choices: They pull back under the train until another storm arrives.
They break off at the switch points and wait for repair crews.
They heat up the steel rails so the joints can expand again.
They drop fine sand across the yard to guide the dispatchers.
qs.why: Paragraph 3 states that the brushes extend when snow falls and "retract back under the train once the track is clean."

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Winter storms make it completely impossible for heavy trains to run safely on steel tracks.
Train drivers should rely on general weather guesses rather than checking real rail measurements.
Rail crews use tools, sensors, and data to manage how freezing weather affects tracks and wheels.
Public transit riders lose trust whenever a train carries sandboxes or heaters during January.
qs.why: Every paragraph explains a specific winter challenge and the engineering tools or data crews use to keep trains running.

clues.text: shrinking slightly and pulling tight at every joint
the firm hold between wheel and rail that keeps steel from spinning in place
stretching far longer than a quick storm
